content: 1. The number of deaths can be compared to the number of people living with HIV to analyze trends over time. This comparison is essential for understanding the impact of HIV prevention and treatment programs. 2. Monitoring trends in HIV-related deaths and prevalence is critical for detecting shifts in patterns and projecting future needs. This analysis should consider factors such as sex, age, mode of transmission (especially for children), key populations, other target groups, and geographic location. 3. Estimates of HIV prevalence and trends should be calculated using internationally consistent modeling approaches, cohort studies, and age-specific HIV prevalence data. These methods help predict the direction of the epidemic. 4. Data collection and disaggregation by age, sex, key populations, location, and pregnancy or breastfeeding status are essential for analyzing specific indicators. This disaggregation allows for targeted responses to maximize the impact of HIV programs. 5. Confidentiality must be maintained during data collection, particularly for key populations who face stigma and discrimination. All data should be securely stored, and staff must be trained to handle data with confidentiality. 6. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems may need to be adapted to align with updated guidelines. This includes consolidating and prioritizing indicators, investing in data sources and surveillance, planning for data disaggregation, and building capacity for linked data analysis across the health sector. 7. Data should be used for decision-making during regular program reviews. Evaluating the impact of each stage of the care cascade on outcomes is necessary to improve the response and adapt M&E systems to support differentiated care models. 8. Routine patient monitoring and case reporting form the foundation of data required to measure the cascade of HIV services over time. Robust M&E systems are needed to track enrollment, retention, and outcomes in HIV care. 9. Facility and outreach reporting systems collect data continuously. This includes patient monitoring data from individual records, case reporting data from newly diagnosed HIV cases, and outreach data from NGOs and community health workers. 10. Administrative sources, such as financial and health systems data, facility lists, and key policies, provide additional information for monitoring HIV programs. 11. Population-based surveys, such as demographic and health surveys or integrated biological and behavioral surveillance surveys, are periodically conducted to gather data on general and key populations. 12. Facility assessments, including service availability and readiness surveys, and sentinel surveillance data, provide insights into the capacity and performance of health facilities. 13. Vital registration systems, which record births and deaths, can include information on the cause of death, contributing to the understanding of HIV-related mortality. 14. The ultimate goal of M&E is to provide data for decision-makers at all stages of the HIV program cycle. Regular program reviews and systematic evaluations are necessary to assess performance and inform policy improvements. 15. Cascade analysis supports the identification of trends, progress, gaps, and bottlenecks in service delivery. This analysis links individual indicators to outcomes and impacts, helping to develop solutions and improve services. 16. Monitoring antiretroviral (ARV) drug toxicity is essential as more people experience prolonged exposure to these drugs. Toxicity is a common reason for non-adherence, treatment discontinuation, or drug substitution. 17. Routine monitoring provides data on the incidence and clinical significance of ARV toxicities and their impact on adherence, outcomes, and retention. WHO recommends complementing routine monitoring with active sentinel toxicity surveillance. 18. Countries should integrate toxicity monitoring into national M&E systems using a standardized approach. This includes defining a minimum set of data elements for reporting on the magnitude of toxicities and their impact on treatment. 19. Special considerations for pregnant and breastfeeding women include monitoring maternal adverse outcomes, adverse birth outcomes (e.g., stillbirths, preterm births, congenital anomalies), and infant health outcomes (e.g., growth and development). 20. Surveillance for ARV-related toxicity during pregnancy and breastfeeding involves prospective monitoring of mother-infant pairs and assessing birth outcomes through registries and surveillance systems. 21. Drug resistance surveillance is critical as the emergence of HIV drug resistance (HIV-DR) threatens the effectiveness of antiretroviral therapy (ART). WHO recommends integrating HIV-DR prevention and assessment into national HIV programs. 22. Routine monitoring of early warning indicators (EWIs) for HIV-DR, such as on-time ARV drug pickup, retention on ART, drug stock-outs, and viral load suppression, helps identify conditions favoring virological failure and resistance. 23. WHO provides guidance on conducting special studies and surveillance for ARV drug toxicity and resistance, including active surveillance within sentinel cohorts and during pregnancy and breastfeeding. 24. EWIs are clinic-level quality-of-care indicators that alert managers to conditions favoring resistance. Achieving optimal performance on these indicators minimizes preventable HIV-DR and maximizes long-term viral suppression. 25. Routine program data should be the primary source for EWI reporting. However, if routine data coverage is insufficient, results may be useful at subnational levels to inform and improve local programs.
